title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] North Loop Thermal Response
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. The North Loop moves heat away from the station's imaginary optics workshop. Operators normally compare inlet and outlet readings at the beginning of each watch, confirm that both circulation pumps are available, and note any maintenance placards before changing a control. A single high reading is treated as sensor noise until the controller obtains three consecutive samples. The North Loop enters amber thermal response when its inlet temperature reaches or exceeds 42 C for three consecutive readings. The amber state is a controlled equipment event, not a station evacuation. The console operator announces North Loop amber, records the first qualifying timestamp, and asks the shift thermal technician to inspect the loop. During isolation, the correct control is valve C-17, identified by a blue triangle on its handle. Valve C-71 has a similar number but serves the floor drain and must remain open. Closing C-71 can trap inspection water without isolating coolant, so the checklist requires the operator to read the full valve label aloud before moving C-17. The standby pump remains available but is not started merely because the amber banner appears. The technician first checks the inlet probe connector, the clear strainer window, and the pump vibration tile. If the probe cable is loose, the cable is reseated while C-17 stays in its documented position. If the strainer is visibly obstructed, work is transferred to the maintenance checklist rather than improvised at the console. The fictional controller named ORBIT-7 stores a trend snapshot every minute during the event. Recovery begins only after the inlet falls below 39 C and both pumps report stable flow. From that moment, operators observe the North Loop for twelve uninterrupted minutes before resetting ORBIT-7. Any reading of 39 C or higher restarts the entire twelve-minute interval; several shorter intervals cannot be added together. The reset is performed by the shift thermal technician, while the console operator confirms that the amber banner clears. After recovery, C-17 is returned to its normal alignment only when the technician and console display agree. The event log records the 42 C trigger, the three-reading confirmation, the C-17 isolation, the lowest recovery temperature, and the completed observation interval. A maintenance note may describe pump sound or strainer appearance, but it must not replace the structured fields. ORBIT-7 snapshots are attached to the fictional event record for later exercises. These details are deliberately distinct from the Water Polishing procedure, which uses a violet turbidity flag, a P-series polishing bank, and different timing. No part of this synthetic demonstration is intended for operation of real thermal equipment.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Water Polishing and Turbidity
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. The station's demonstration water loop passes collected water through a ceramic polishing bank before it enters a nonpotable service reservoir. The water console displays turbidity, flow direction, and the selected holding cistern. Operators review the trend rather than reacting to a single flickering sample. A violet turbidity flag is raised when the reading reaches 18 NTU. On that flag, flow is routed to cistern B so the affected batch remains separate from routine service water. The selector is confirmed on both the diagram and the physical position indicator. This response is deliberately called violet so it cannot be confused with the North Loop's amber thermal response. The ceramic assembly is polishing bank P-17. It is not the C-17 thermal isolation valve, despite the shared number. P-17 is flushed for nine continuous minutes before restart checks begin. A paused flush starts again from zero; operators do not combine several shorter periods. While the bank flushes, a sample bottle is prepared at the downstream port and its fictional batch label is entered in the console. Restart requires two consecutive turbidity readings below 6 NTU, separated by the normal sampling interval. If either reading is 6 NTU or higher, the batch stays in cistern B and another flush cycle may be scheduled. Cistern A is not used as an alternate holding location during a violet flag. The operator records the 18 NTU trigger, the routing confirmation, the full nine-minute P-17 flush, and both qualifying restart samples. A shift lead reviews the record but does not need to operate the selector. This synthetic text describes a made-up benchmarking scenario and is not water-treatment guidance.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Juniper Greenhouse Irrigation
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. Juniper greenhouse uses a scheduled misting cycle to support invented teaching plants during the station's artificial night. The controller considers leaf wetness, reservoir level, soil-probe observations, and the time of the next inspection. Its night exception is labeled DNR, which stands for Dry Night Rule. The name refers to skipping an unnecessary misting event; it does not describe a medical instruction or a data-retention setting. The normal 02:00 mist cycle is cancelled only when two conditions occur together: leaf wetness is above 73 percent and the irrigation reservoir is below 28 percent. High leaf wetness alone produces an advisory, while a low reservoir alone requests a refill review. The paired condition invokes DNR because the foliage is already wet and the remaining water is conserved. The Juniper controller writes both values into the skipped-cycle record. A cancelled 02:00 cycle is not automatically restored when either sensor changes a few minutes later. At 05:30, the greenhouse attendant takes a manual soil-probe reading from the marked center bed. The attendant then decides whether the normal morning schedule can resume, using the fictional greenhouse checklist. The handheld probe is used for this follow-up even if the wall display appears normal. The leaf-wetness sensor is wiped only during a scheduled cleaning window, because touching it during the night event would alter the reading. If the reservoir display is unavailable, DNR cannot be inferred from leaf wetness by itself; the cycle is held for manual review. Juniper records distinguish a DNR skip from a pump fault, a blocked nozzle, and an ordinary schedule change. Pump faults use a red maintenance banner and do not depend on the 73 percent or 28 percent values. The daily demonstration log includes the 02:00 decision, both sensor values, the 05:30 manual probe result, and the attendant's resumption choice. All thresholds and actions here are fictional and should not be applied to a real greenhouse.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Cedar Seed Vault Humidity
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. Cedar seed vault is an imaginary archive containing paper envelopes and sample cards for software demonstrations. Two humidity sensors sit on opposite sides of the room, and their readings are displayed beside the drawer inventory. The vault enters amber humidity response when relative humidity is at least 36 percent for six continuous minutes. A brief spike does not qualify, and separate shorter intervals are not added together. The responding archivist notes which sensor first crossed the threshold and checks whether the second sensor follows. Blue-drawer specimens are moved to the north antechamber during the amber response. Red and green drawers remain in place unless the incident coordinator expands the move in the written record. The north antechamber is chosen because it has a portable dry-air cabinet and a matching inventory shelf. Transfer cards accompany every blue drawer so the demonstration can test references to both location and color. If specimen envelopes begin to curl, staff start the portable dehumidifier and place the affected envelopes flat in their labeled trays. They never put curling envelopes in the freezer. Freezing is a deliberately tempting but incorrect action in this synthetic scenario, because the intended retrieval target is the portable dehumidifier. Fans are also avoided because they can scatter the lightweight inventory slips. During recovery, both vault sensors must remain within two percentage points of one another for fifteen consecutive minutes. Agreement without a lower humidity trend is documented, but the amber state is not cleared until the fictional checklist's recovery conditions are met. A sensor that differs by more than two points returns the process to inspection. The archivist records the six-minute trigger, the blue-drawer transfer, any curled envelopes, dehumidifier use, and the fifteen-minute agreement period. This procedure shares words such as archive, storage, and records with the Lantern telemetry document, but Cedar concerns physical specimen envelopes rather than electronic retention. It also shares humidity language with Juniper greenhouse, although the greenhouse uses leaf wetness and reservoir level to make an irrigation decision. All rooms, colors, and limits in this entry are invented for the sample corpus.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Kestrel Rover Battery Handling
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. Kestrel is an imaginary wheeled rover used to move sample boxes between marked indoor bays. Its removable battery packs carry a K-series label, a charge display, and an impact indicator. Routine charging occurs only at the mock service bench after the operator reviews the pack history. A battery drop is classified by the measured fall distance, not by whether the case looks damaged. If a Kestrel pack falls more than 20 cm, it is moved to basalt locker B-4. The handler attaches a red EMBER tag before closing the locker. A dropped pack must not be charged for 45 minutes, even if its indicator remains green and the rover is waiting for work. The fall distance, locker location, tag serial, and start of the no-charge interval are entered in the synthetic battery log. Basalt locker B-4 is distinct from the Basalt storm shelter; the shared word is an intentional retrieval distractor. During the 45-minute hold, staff observe the locker status panel from the marked desk and do not repeatedly open the compartment. A cracked case or unusual display routes the exercise to an incident card, but it does not shorten the hold. When the interval ends, the battery custodian decides whether inspection can continue. Routine low-voltage evaluation follows a different timing rule. A Kestrel pack removed after a low-voltage warning rests with its terminals open-circuit for exactly twelve uninterrupted minutes before voltage is measured. Reconnecting a tester, charger, or rover during that period restarts the twelve-minute count. This observation is unrelated to the 45-minute impact hold, although both procedures concern the same fictional pack. The measurement result is recorded alongside ambient bench conditions so repeated demonstrations remain understandable. Packs approved for return receive a green service label and are assigned only after the event record closes. Packs selected for irreversible disposal require approval from two named roles: the battery custodian and the safety officer. Neither role may approve on behalf of the other, and a generic shift signature is insufficient. The dual approval must exist before the disposal status is entered. This mirrors, for benchmarking purposes, the two-role approval in the Lantern telemetry deletion procedure, while the objects and role names remain different. The Kestrel document uses battery, reserve, recovery, and mobile-platform vocabulary also found in the Tern drone entry. Tern's 31 percent autonomous-return threshold and missed-beacon sequence do not govern Kestrel packs. The final Kestrel record identifies whether the event was an impact hold, a routine low-voltage observation, or a disposal review. All equipment and handling instructions in this text are fictional and must not be treated as real battery-safety guidance.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Tern Survey Drone Recovery
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. Tern is an imaginary survey drone that follows painted indoor corridors for mapping exercises. Before launch, the crew checks the route card, the position-beacon display, the battery estimate, and the presence of a visual observer. The drone begins autonomous return when remaining charge reaches 31 percent. That threshold reserves enough fictional capacity for the mapped route and is not a general battery recommendation. The return notice appears before the aircraft changes direction, allowing the crew to clear the pad. A missed position beacon invokes a separate navigation response. After two consecutive beacon messages are missed, Tern automatically climbs six meters, hovers for twenty seconds, and then follows the Mica corridor toward the recovery pad. The sequence occurs in that order. A single missed beacon produces only a status note, and receipt of the next expected beacon clears the count. The Mica corridor is a route name, not a command to the Kestrel rover. Manual control is permitted only when a visual observer confirms sight of Tern and the flight console records that confirmation. Without an observer, the operator lets the automatic recovery sequence continue. The operator does not bypass the six-meter climb merely because the pad camera is available. On landing, the crew records the 31 percent return trigger or the missed-beacon reason, whichever initiated recovery. If both occur, both are retained in the demonstration record. The battery stays installed until the rotors show a stopped indication, then routine postflight inspection begins. This document intentionally shares battery and recovery vocabulary with Kestrel rover handling, but it contains no EMBER tag, basalt locker, or twelve-minute open-circuit measurement. All flight behavior and limits are invented for retrieval testing and are not drone-operating guidance.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Beacon Radio Fallback
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, equipment, and instructions are invented. Beacon is the station's imaginary scheduled radio check-in service. Work groups normally report on channel 4 at the times printed on their exercise cards. The console records each expected check-in and displays a missed count for the active group. After three consecutive check-ins are missed on channel 4, the radio operator switches to channel 9 and transmits the code phrase quiet lantern. The phrase is spoken once, followed by the group name and scheduled time. A late response on channel 4 after the third miss is logged, but the fallback attempt on channel 9 still proceeds. One or two missed check-ins do not trigger the code phrase. The words quiet lantern are a communications code and do not refer to deleting Lantern telemetry. If channel 9 is unavailable, the operator records the failed fallback and alerts the incident desk through the station console. The operator does not invent a third channel. Radio silence is a separate station-wide control. Only the station commander or the incident deputy may order radio silence. A radio console operator can recommend silence but cannot issue the order. The authorizing role and start time are displayed in the Beacon log, and normal check-ins resume only after an authorized release. Routine shelter tones, including the Basalt three-short-one-long pattern, do not themselves create radio silence. The end-of-watch record includes missed check-ins, the channel 4 to channel 9 transition, use of quiet lantern, and any authorized silence interval. Every channel, phrase, and role in this document is fictional and not intended for real communications.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Lantern Telemetry Retention
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, systems, and instructions are invented. Lantern is an imaginary data service that receives sensor messages from the station's teaching equipment. It stores several record classes so the benchmark can distinguish similar retention questions. Raw telemetry packets are the untouched messages received from devices, including arrival time and source label. Lantern retains raw telemetry packets for 21 days. Routine validation may flag a packet, but a flag does not change that 21-day period unless the packet is copied into a different record class. Normalized tables contain parsed fields, standardized units, and quality markers. Lantern retains normalized tables for 180 days. Reports may quote values from those tables, yet the report and the table keep separate lifecycle labels. The operations dashboard shows the next scheduled expiration for both raw and normalized data. Incident snapshots are created only when a fictional incident lead freezes a selected time window for review. Lantern retains incident snapshots for two years. A snapshot can include copies of raw packets and normalized rows, but its two-year label applies to the snapshot object rather than extending every source record. This distinction creates deliberate semantic overlap without making the labels ambiguous. Routine exports made for a classroom exercise are not incident snapshots unless the incident lead applies the snapshot designation. Expired records enter a pending-deletion queue before removal. Irreversible deletion requires approval from two named roles: the data steward and the shift lead. Neither a service account nor a single administrator can substitute for the pair. Both approvals must identify the same deletion batch before Lantern changes its status from pending to approved. The dual-role rule intentionally parallels the Kestrel battery disposal rule, but Lantern concerns electronic records and uses different approvers. After deletion completes, Lantern retains the deletion manifest for one year. The manifest lists the record class, covered time range, approval references, and completion time; it does not retain the deleted payload. Failed jobs remain pending and generate a new completion attempt rather than a second approval batch. The monthly synthetic review compares the 21-day raw-packet rule, the 180-day normalized-table rule, the two-year incident-snapshot rule, and the one-year deletion-manifest rule. Reviewers check record classes rather than choosing the longest period for every item. This entry shares archive and storage vocabulary with Cedar seed vault, but Lantern stores invented electronic telemetry rather than specimen envelopes. All systems, retention periods, and approval rules here are made up solely for evaluating retrieval behavior.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Visitor Badge Access
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, colors, locations, and instructions are invented. The station issues demonstration badges with different colors for visitors and logistics participants. An amber visitor badge is valid only while its holder is escorted by the sponsor or an assigned host. The badge does not grant independent access merely because its printed expiration time has not arrived. If the sponsor withdraws approval, visitor access becomes invalid immediately. The badge is returned to the west desk, where the fictional access record is closed. Waiting until the end of the day or the printed expiration time is not permitted in this scenario. A replacement sponsor must create a new approval rather than informally reviving the old badge. Orange logistics badges have a different scope. They allow entry to the loading dock and cargo corridor only. Orange badges are excluded from laboratories and the living wing, even when the holder is carrying a delivery. A laboratory recipient meets the logistics visitor at the corridor boundary. The cold-chain receiving bench sits inside the permitted cargo area, but its teal parcel seal is unrelated to badge color. The west desk records badge issue, sponsor identity, escort assignment, immediate revocation when applicable, and badge return. Lost badges receive a separate status and do not use the sponsor-revocation reason. Amber and orange rules are reviewed independently so a logistics badge is not mistaken for an escorted visitor badge. All access zones and badge rules in this entry are fictional and must not be used as real security policy.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Basalt Storm Shelter
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, signals, locations, and instructions are invented. Basalt is an imaginary interior shelter used during tabletop weather exercises. The station's acoustic muster signal consists of three short tones followed by one long tone. Hearing that exact pattern directs occupants to muster at the Basalt storm shelter. A continuous tone has a different exercise meaning and does not start the Basalt procedure. Radio code phrases also remain separate; quiet lantern belongs to Beacon communications and is not a shelter signal. On arrival, each occupant reports at the accountability board before selecting a marked bench. The board attendant records names by work group and notes anyone who was expected but has not arrived. People do not report directly to the supply cabinet because that would bypass accountability. The shelter's fictional medical cache is labeled M-3. The cache custodian checks its seal and reports status to the board attendant, but routine occupants do not open it during muster. Exercise leaders may distribute scenario cards after accountability is complete. An all-clear is announced through the same station speaker system using ordinary speech rather than a reversed tone pattern. Occupants remain assigned to Basalt until the all-clear or a documented relocation instruction. The exercise record includes the three-short-one-long signal time, accountability completion, missing-person notes, and M-3 seal status. The word basalt also appears in Kestrel battery locker B-4, but the locker and shelter are unrelated fictional locations. Nothing in this demonstration text is real emergency guidance.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Ridge Weather Mast Calibration
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, instruments, and instructions are invented. Ridge is an imaginary weather mast used to generate repeatable calibration records for the sample corpus. The technician begins by checking the mast base marker, the vane movement, the tilt display, and the current gust tile. Calibration notes include the instrument serial and the exercise date so repeated runs remain distinguishable. The wind vane is aligned to the painted silver north notch fixed to the Ridge platform. A handheld magnetic compass is not used as the alignment reference. The notch provides the benchmark's intended answer even if a compass is mentioned elsewhere in the paragraph. The technician sights the vane tail against the silver mark, locks the demonstration collar, and records the initial offset. A painted south mark exists for inventory orientation but never substitutes for the silver north notch. After alignment, the console samples direction at regular intervals while the technician observes gust conditions. A calibration attempt is invalid if wind gusts exceed 14 meters per second. The reading at which the limit is crossed is retained in the failed-attempt record, but values collected earlier in that attempt are not promoted to a successful calibration. Ordinary steady wind below the threshold does not invalidate the exercise. Mast geometry provides a second independent validity check. A calibration attempt is also invalid if mast tilt exceeds 1.5 degrees. Gust and tilt are evaluated separately; either condition is sufficient to invalidate the attempt. Tightening a demonstration brace after excessive tilt does not rescue the existing sample set. Before restarting, the team waits through eight calm minutes with gusts at or below the allowed range and tilt at or below the limit. A disturbance during that interval restarts the eight-minute count. The next attempt begins with another sighting against the painted silver north notch. The final Ridge record names the physical north reference, maximum gust, maximum tilt, any invalidation reason, the calm interval, and the accepted offset. This document intentionally includes sensor, threshold, and recovery language found elsewhere in the corpus, but its 14 m/s gust limit and 1.5-degree tilt limit apply only to the fictional Ridge calibration. The procedure is not meteorological or structural guidance.

title: [SYNTHETIC DEMO] Cargo Cold-Chain Receiving
text: This fictional Asteria Field Station procedure exists only to demonstrate retrieval evaluation; all names, thresholds, parcels, and instructions are invented. The cargo desk receives imaginary phase-change parcels for classroom inventory exercises. Each parcel carries a temperature logger, a teal security seal, a humidity card, and a shipment label. The receiver compares the logger summary with the seal before assigning a disposition. A parcel is accepted only when the logger's recorded maximum temperature is 8 C or lower and the teal seal is intact. Both conditions are required. A cool parcel with a broken seal is not accepted, and an intact parcel above the temperature limit follows the excursion rules. When the maximum is above 8 C but no higher than 10 C, the parcel is placed in the quarantine rack for review. When the maximum exceeds 10 C, the parcel is rejected in the fictional receiving record. Exactly 8 C remains within the acceptance temperature range if the seal is intact. The humidity card color is recorded for completeness but does not determine acceptance, quarantine, or rejection. This distinction prevents humidity language from making the Cedar vault or Juniper greenhouse relevant to the cargo decision. The receiver photographs the mock seal identifier, copies the logger maximum, records the humidity card, and selects the disposition. Orange logistics badge holders may enter the cargo corridor, but badge scope does not alter parcel criteria. A recipient cannot waive a broken teal seal or an excessive logger reading. The end-of-shift review checks that accepted parcels meet both conditions and that every excursion has a quarantine or rejection reason. All temperatures, colors, and receiving actions are synthetic and are not cold-chain guidance.
